title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud enabled by AI-generated content. Scammers fabricated a news article depicting a real interview between two named public figures, neither of whom participated, and used it to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure is not a malfunction of a legitimate deployed system but a deliberate misuse of AI tools, specifically deepfake and synthetic text generation, to produce convincing false material at scale.

The deception operated across multiple layers: fake articles, fake reviews, fake websites, and fake advertisements were combined to create a self-reinforcing appearance of legitimacy. This layered approach means no single point of content moderation would catch the whole scheme, and the platforms hosting individual pieces may not see the full pattern. ASIC's figures show the volume of such content is growing sharply, which indicates that whatever detection or removal processes exist are not keeping pace with production.

What is not established is who created the specific fabricated article, what AI tools were used to produce it, or whether any platform knowingly hosted it. ASIC's figures describe removals and trends, not prosecutions or findings of liability against any particular party.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has exposed a rising scam trend. The fabricated story promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, by claiming Bullock became upset discussing it. The interview never occurred. Scammers are increasingly using AI-generated deepfakes and fake content to impersonate celebrities and politicians to promote fraudulent investments. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows these schemes are becoming more sophisticated and convincing.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated figure, followed by other politicians and financial experts like Alan Kohler. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, reviews, websites, and advertisements to lure investors. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through its free public registers before investing. Alan Kohler has called for heavy fines against platforms hosting this content and the AI models that create it.
